---
title: 'Automate Oore'
status: implemented
description: 'Drive Oore from a script, a CI job or an AI agent: sign in with an API token, run a build, wait for it, read why it failed, and hand out the install link.'
---

Everything the web UI does goes through the Oore HTTP API, so a script or an
agent can do the same work without a browser. This page walks through the
daily loop three ways: with the `oore` CLI, with `curl`, and with the
[`@oore/client`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@oore/client) JavaScript
client. Pick whichever your tool already speaks.

An agent that reads documentation should start from
[`llms.txt`](https://docs.oore.build/llms.txt). Every page on this site is also
plain Markdown: add `.md` to its address, or send `Accept: text/markdown`.

## 1. Create an API token

Scripts sign in with an API token, not with your browser session. Open
**Settings > API tokens**, select **Create token**, give it a name that says
where it runs, such as `release-bot` or `claude-code on my laptop`, pick the
**Developer** role, and keep the suggested 90 day expiry. Copy the token: Oore
shows it once.

[API tokens](/team/api-tokens) explains roles, expiry, revoking, and how to
keep a token out of a repository.

## 2. Point your tools at the instance

Oore is self-hosted, so every tool needs the address of your instance and the
token. Set two variables:

```bash
export OORE_URL='https://ci.example.com'
export OORE_TOKEN='<token from step 1>'
```

The `oore` CLI, `oore-dev` and the examples on this site read these names.
`oore` also reads the older `OORE_DAEMON_URL` and `OORE_SESSION_TOKEN`, and
`--url` and `--token` on the command line win over both. Keep the token in a
secret store or your shell's keychain helper, not in a file you commit.

If the instance sits behind an access proxy that wants its own credentials,
such as a Cloudflare Access service token, give the CLI the extra headers, one
`Name: value` per line:

```bash
export OORE_HTTP_HEADERS='CF-Access-Client-Id: <id>
CF-Access-Client-Secret: <secret>'
```

`curl` takes the same headers with `-H`, and `@oore/client` with the `headers`
option of `createOoreClient`.

Check the connection:

```bash
oore status --json
curl -fsS "$OORE_URL/v1/users/me" -H "Authorization: Bearer $OORE_TOKEN"
```

## 3. Find the pipeline

Builds start from a pipeline. List apps and their pipelines to find its ID:

```bash
oore project list
oore pipeline list --project FlutterShop
```

```bash
curl -fsS "$OORE_URL/v1/projects?search=FlutterShop" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $OORE_TOKEN"
curl -fsS "$OORE_URL/v1/projects/$PROJECT_ID/pipelines" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $OORE_TOKEN"
```

`--project` and `--pipeline` take a name or an ID. When a name matches more
than one, the CLI stops and lists the matches with their IDs.

## 4. Run a build and wait for it

```bash
oore build run --project FlutterShop --pipeline Release --branch main --wait
```

`--wait` follows the build to its result and exits with the build's
[exit code](#exit-codes). Add `--json` to get the finished build as one JSON
object on standard output.

With `curl`, queue the build, then ask for it until its `status` is final
(`succeeded`, `failed`, `canceled`, `timed_out` or `expired`):

```bash
build_id=$(curl -fsS -X POST "$OORE_URL/v1/projects/$PROJECT_ID/builds" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $OORE_TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d "{\"pipeline_id\": \"$PIPELINE_ID\", \"branch\": \"main\"}" | jq -r .build.id)

while :; do
  status=$(curl -fsS "$OORE_URL/v1/builds/$build_id" \
    -H "Authorization: Bearer $OORE_TOKEN" | jq -r .status)
  case "$status" in
    succeeded|failed|canceled|timed_out|expired) break ;;
  esac
  sleep 10
done
echo "$status"
```

A newer daemon also answers `GET /v1/builds/{build_id}?wait=60` only when the
build changes or the minute is up, so a loop needs no `sleep`.

With `@oore/client`:

```ts
import { createBuild, createOoreClient, getBuild } from '@oore/client'

const client = createOoreClient({
  baseUrl: process.env.OORE_URL!,
  token: process.env.OORE_TOKEN,
})

const { build } = await createBuild({
  client,
  path: { project_id: projectId },
  body: { pipeline_id: pipelineId, branch: 'main' },
})

const done = new Set([
  'succeeded',
  'failed',
  'canceled',
  'timed_out',
  'expired',
])
let current = build
while (!done.has(current.status)) {
  await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, 10_000))
  current = await getBuild({ client, path: { build_id: build.id } })
}
```

A webhook tells you when a build finishes without asking at all. See
[Outbound webhooks](/reference/webhooks).

## 5. Read why a build failed

```bash
oore build why "$build_id"
```

It prints the failed step and its exit code, the likely cause and fix, the
last 40 lines of that step's log and the failed tests. `--json` gives the same
as one object, which is the easiest thing to hand to an agent.

With `curl`, the likely cause and the log are separate calls:

```bash
curl -fsS "$OORE_URL/v1/builds/$build_id/failure-hint" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $OORE_TOKEN"
curl -fsS "$OORE_URL/v1/builds/$build_id/logs" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $OORE_TOKEN"
```

A newer daemon puts them together at `GET /v1/builds/{build_id}/diagnosis`,
and the logs take `step`, `tail` and `search` so you fetch only the part you
need.

## 6. Get the install link

```bash
oore build install-link "$build_id" --platform android
```

With `curl`, list the build's artifacts and ask for a link to one:

```bash
artifact_id=$(curl -fsS "$OORE_URL/v1/builds/$build_id/artifacts" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $OORE_TOKEN" | jq -r '.artifacts[0].id')
curl -fsS -X POST "$OORE_URL/v1/artifacts/$artifact_id/install-link" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $OORE_TOKEN"
```

The answer holds `install_url`, a page a tester opens on the phone, and
`expires_at`. With `@oore/client`, the same calls are `listArtifacts` and
`createArtifactInstallLink`.

## Exit codes

Every `oore` command uses the same exit codes, so a script can branch on them
without reading the output:

| Code | Meaning                                                                 |
| ---- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| 0    | Done                                                                    |
| 1    | Failed: the build did not succeed, or the command hit an error          |
| 2    | Blocked: a person must act, for example to approve a build or fix setup |
| 3    | The store refused the upload or the release                             |
| 4    | Not signed in, or the token may not do this                             |
| 5    | Not found                                                               |
| 64   | The command was used wrongly                                            |

With `--json`, standard output holds only JSON, and a failure prints one JSON
object on standard error:

```json
{
  "error": "Build not found",
  "code": "not_found",
  "status": 404,
  "hint": "Check the build ID with `oore build list`."
}
```

`code` is the API's error code when the failure came from the API. The codes
are listed under [Error codes](/reference/errors).

Without a terminal, the CLI never stops to ask a question. A command that
would ask for confirmation, such as a delete, needs `--yes`.

## Retry safely

An agent that times out and tries again must not start a second build. Send an
`Idempotency-Key` header with a value you make up for that one action, such
as a UUID, on calls that start work: create build, re-run, send to testers,
release actions and promote. Oore keeps the key for 24 hours. The same key
with the same body answers with the first response and starts nothing. The
CLI sends a key for you.

```bash
curl -fsS -X POST "$OORE_URL/v1/projects/$PROJECT_ID/builds" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $OORE_TOKEN" \
  -H "Idempotency-Key: $(uuidgen)" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d "{\"pipeline_id\": \"$PIPELINE_ID\"}"
```
